section_title: How do signs, an image and a mark enforce worship of the beast?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 11 Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. This beast had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon. 12 And this beast exercised all the authority of the first beast and caused the earth and those who dwell in it to worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed. 13 And the second beast performed great signs, even causing fire from heaven to come down to earth in the presence of the people. 14 Because of the signs it was given to perform on behalf of the first beast, it deceived those who dwell on the earth, telling them to make an image to the beast that had been wounded by the sword and yet had lived.

15 The second beast was permitted to give breath to the image of the first beast, so that the image could speak and cause all who refused to worship it to be killed. 16 And the second beast required all people, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a mark on their right hand or on their forehead, 17 so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark—the name of the beast or the number of its name.
18 Here is a call for wisdom: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666.

context_lines: A second beast rises from the earth. It has horns like a lamb but speaks like a dragon. Its appearance and voice point in different directions. Its actions reveal its purpose: it exercises the first beast’s authority and leads people to worship that beast.

Its signs include fire descending from heaven in public view. These displays deceive people and support the making of an image of the first beast. The image is given breath and can speak, and those who refuse to worship it face death. The account links the signs with the false worship they promote.

The pressure also reaches ordinary economic life. People of every social standing are required to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, and buying or selling depends on having it. The Greek word charagma means a stamped or impressed mark; see [Thayer’s entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/5480.htm). Here its meaning is supplied by the surrounding scene: it identifies people with the beast’s name or the number of its name.

The chapter ends by calling for wisdom and understanding to calculate the number, 666. The number belongs within the account of the beast, its name and the allegiance it demands. John gives a challenge to discernment rather than an explanation of the mark’s physical manufacture.
common_interpretation_lines: [Walvoord](https://swartzentrover.com/cotor/E-Books/holiness/Walvoord/Revelation/Rev_13.htm) expects a future false prophet supporting the first beast, with the mark identifying its worshipers. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/) connects the mark with acknowledgment of papal authority and succession. The [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/revelation/13) place the second beast within the setting of false prophecy and pressure to worship the emperor. These readings differ over the setting while recognizing the connection between deception, worship and coercion.

The number also receives different explanations. The USCCB notes favor a calculation using Caesar Nero’s name in Hebrew letters. Wesley takes 666 as a period of years. Walvoord favors its significance as a human number falling short of divine perfection. These are proposed explanations; the passage itself gives the number and the instruction to calculate.

An early Christian discussion shows why caution is appropriate. In [Against Heresies 5.30](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103530.htm), Irenaeus considers several Greek names that total 666, but declines to pronounce a certain name. Letter values were therefore not confined to Hebrew, and obtaining the total does not by itself establish an identification.
god_plan_lines: The forced worship of an image recalls [Daniel 3:4–6 and 16–18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/daniel/3.htm). There, a ruler commands people of many nations and languages to worship his statue under threat of death. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refuse, whether or not God delivers them. Revelation continues that recognizable conflict between imposed worship and faithfulness to God.

The deceptive signs also fit the warning in [2 Thessalonians 2:8–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_thessalonians/2.htm), where satanic power and wonders accompany rejection of the truth. The same passage promises the lawless one’s defeat by Jesus. The wider picture joins discernment with hope: a display of power does not establish that its message comes from God, and the power opposing Him will not endure.
